1.1: When Philopator heard from those returning that Antioḵos had taken control of the territories that belonged to him, he ordered all his infantry and cavalry to assemble, took his sister Arsinoe with him, and marched as far as the region of Raphia, where Antioḵos and his army were camped.
1.2: Theodotos, determined to carry out his plan, took with him the bravest soldiers previously entrusted to him by Ptolemaeus, and at night made his way to Ptolemaeus’ tent to kill him on his own initiative and end the war.
1.3: But Dositheos, known as the son of Drimylos, a Yahuḏi by birth but later a renegade from the Torah and customs of his people, secretly took Ptolemaeus away and had another man lie in his place in the tent. That man ended up suffering the fate intended for Ptolemaeus.
1.4: A fierce battle broke out. Antioḵos’ men were winning. Arsinoe moved up and down the ranks, her hair disheveled, weeping and pleading with the soldiers to fight bravely for themselves, their children, and their wives, promising that if they won, she would give each of them two minas of gold.
1.5: As a result, their enemies were defeated in close combat, and many of them were taken captive.
1.6: After overcoming this threat, the meleḵ decided to visit the nearby cities to encourage them.
1.7: By doing this, and by making gifts to their temples, he inspired confidence among his subjects.
1.8: The Yahuḏim sent some of their council members and elders to him. Their previous greetings, gifts, and congratulations made him even more eager to visit their city.
1.9: When he arrived at Yerushalayim, he offered sacrifices and thank-offerings to the Greatest Elohim, did everything appropriate for the qodesh place, and entered the inner court.
1.10: He was so impressed by the magnificence of the place and so amazed by the orderliness of the Miqdash that he considered entering the qodesh place itself.
1.11: When he was told that this was not allowed—that no one from the nation, not even the kohenim in general, but only the kohĕn ha’gadol who presides over them all, and only once a year, could enter—he refused to accept it.
1.12: They read the Torah to him, but he insisted on going in, claiming he should be allowed. He said, “Even if others are denied this honor, I shouldn’t be.”
1.13: He asked why, when he entered all the other temples, none of the kohenim there stopped him.
1.14: Someone answered him clearly, telling him he was wrong to boast about this.
1.15: He replied, “Well, since I have done this elsewhere, whatever the reason, shouldn’t I enter here too, with or without your permission?”
1.16: When the kohenim fell down in their qodesh garments, pleading with the Greatest Elohim to help in this time of need and to stop the violence of the fierce aggressor, they filled the Miqdash with cries and tears.
1.17: Those who had stayed behind in the city were terrified and rushed out, not knowing what would happen.
1.18: Young women who had been shut in their rooms came out with their mothers, throwing dust and ashes on their heads and filling the streets with cries.
1.19: Women who had just been prepared for marriage left their bridal chambers, set aside their modesty, and ran through the city in confusion.
1.20: Newborn babies were left behind by their mothers or nurses—some in houses, some in fields; now, with unstoppable urgency, they all gathered at the Most High Miqdash.
1.21: Many different prayers were offered by those gathered there because of the meleḵ’s profane attempt.
1.22: Some of the citizens also found courage and refused to submit to his stubbornness and his plan.
1.23: Calling for arms and to die bravely defending the Torah of their ancestors, they caused a great uproar in the place, and only with difficulty did the elders and aged bring them back to their place of prayer.
1.24: During all this, the crowd kept praying.
1.25: The elders around the meleḵ tried in many ways to turn his proud mind away from his plan.
1.26: But he, stubborn and unmoved by any argument, kept going forward with his intention.
1.27: Even his own officers, seeing this, joined the Yahuḏim in appealing to Him who has all power to help in this crisis and not ignore such arrogant lawlessness.
1.28: The cries of the assembled crowd were so frequent and intense that an indescribable noise filled the place.
1.29: Not only the people, but even the walls and floor seemed to echo, as if everything would rather die than see the Miqdash defiled.

2.1: Then the kohĕn ha’gadol Shim’on knelt down near the qodesh place, spread out his hands in reverence, and prayed this prayer:
2.2: “𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, Meleḵ of the shamayim, Ruler of all creation, Qodesh among the qodesh, the only Governor, the Almighty—listen to us who are oppressed by a wicked and profane man who boasts in his own strength and confidence.
2.3: You are the Creator of all, the Meleḵ of the universe, a righteous Governor, judging all who act with pride and arrogance.
2.4: You destroyed the former workers of unrighteousness, including the giants who trusted in their own strength and boldness, by covering them with a flood beyond measure.
2.5: You made the Seḏomites—workers of extreme evil, infamous for their wickedness—an example for future generations when You covered them with fire and brimstone.
2.6: You showed Your power when You made the bold Pharaoh, who enslaved Your people, go through many and various plagues.
2.7: You rolled back the depths of the sea over him when he chased with chariots and a great crowd, but gave safe passage to those who trusted in You, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 of all creation.
2.8: They saw and experienced the works of Your hands, and praised You, the Almighty.
2.9: You, O Meleḵ, when You created the vast and limitless earth, chose this city. You made this place qodesh for Your Name, even though You need nothing. You esteemed it with Your esteemed presence, after building it for the esteem of Your great and honorable Name.
2.10: Out of love for the people of Yisra’ĕl, You promised that if we turned away from You, became afflicted, and then came to this house and prayed, You would hear our prayer.
2.11: Truly, You are trustworthy and true.
2.12: You often helped our fathers when they were oppressed and humiliated, and rescued them from great dangers.
2.13: Now, qodesh Meleḵ, see how because of our many and great sins, we are crushed and made subject to our enemies, weak and powerless.
2.14: In our low state, this bold and profane man seeks to defile this qodesh place of Yours, qadosh from the earth for the Name of Your Majesty.
2.15: Your dwelling place, the shamayim of shamayim, is truly unapproachable for humans.
2.16: But since it pleased You to show Your esteem among Your people Yisra’ĕl, You set this place apart.
2.17: Do not punish us through the uncleanness of these men, and do not discipline us through their profanity, so that the lawless will not boast in their rage, or exult in arrogant speech, saying,
2.18: ‘We have trampled the qodesh house, just as we trample houses of idols.’
2.19: Wipe away our sins, remove our errors, and show Your compassion at this time.
2.20: Let Your mercies come quickly to us. Grant us peace, so that the downcast and brokenhearted may praise You with their mouths.”
2.21: At that time, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, who sees all things and is above all Qodesh among the qodesh, heard that fitting prayer and struck down the man who was filled with arrogance and pride.
2.22: He shook him back and forth like a reed in the wind, threw him down on the pavement powerless, with his limbs paralyzed, and by a righteous judgment took away his ability to speak.
2.23: His friends and bodyguards, seeing the swift punishment that had suddenly come upon him, were terrified and, fearing he would die, quickly carried him away.
2.24: When he eventually recovered, this severe punishment did not lead him to repentance, but he left with bitter threats.
2.25: He went to Mitsrayim and became even more wicked through his previously mentioned drinking companions, who had no goodness in them,
2.26: and not satisfied with countless acts of evil, his arrogance grew so much that he spread evil rumors there, and many of his friends, watching his intentions closely, joined in carrying out his will.
2.27: He planned to bring public shame on our people. So he set up a stone pillar in the courtyard and had this inscription engraved on it:
2.28: “Entrance to this temple is forbidden to anyone who will not sacrifice. All the Yahuḏim are to be registered as slaves. Those who resist are to be forcibly seized and put to death.
2.29: Those who are registered are to be marked on their bodies with the ivy-leaf symbol of Dionusos, and reduced to these limited rights.”
2.30: To avoid appearing to hate them all, he had it written below that if any chose to join those initiated in the rites, they would have equal rights with the Alexandrians.
2.31: Some of the city officials, therefore, despising any connection with the city of piety, quickly gave in to the meleḵ, hoping to gain great esteem from a future relationship with him.
2.32: But most were moved by a nobler spirit to hold firmly to their beliefs, and by paying money to live in peace, they tried to avoid being registered,
2.33: looking forward with hope for future help, they despised their own apostates, seeing them as enemies of the nation, and cut them off from fellowship and mutual support.

3.1: When the wicked meleḵ discovered this, he became so enraged that he no longer limited his anger to the Yahuḏim in Alexandria. He put even greater pressure on those living in the countryside, ordering that they be quickly gathered into one place and cruelly put to death.
3.2: While this was happening, a hostile rumor was spread by people who had joined together to harm the Yahuḏim. Their excuse was that the Yahuḏim kept them from following the ordinances of the Torah.
3.3: The Yahuḏim had always shown unwavering loyalty to the melaḵim,
3.4: but because they worshipped Elohim and kept His Torah, they made certain distinctions and avoided some things. Because of this, some people hated them,
3.5: even though their lives were marked by righteousness and they had earned a good reputation among others.
3.6: However, the opinions of the rest of humanity were ignored by the foreigners,
3.7: who talked a lot about how the Yahuḏim separated themselves in worship and in what they ate. They claimed the Yahuḏim were unsociable, opposed to the meleḵ’s interests, and refused to associate with him or his soldiers. By saying these things, they stirred up a lot of hatred against them.
3.8: This sudden uproar and gathering of people was noticed by the Yawanites living in the city, even though the Yahuḏim had never harmed them. But they were powerless to help, since there was oppression everywhere. Still, they encouraged the Yahuḏim in their troubles and hoped things would turn out better.
3.9: They said, 'He who knows all things will not ignore such a great people.'
3.10: Some neighbors, friends, and business partners of the Yahuḏim even secretly met with them, promised to help, and said they would do everything they could for them.
3.11: Meanwhile, the meleḵ, proud of his success and not recognizing the superior power of Elohim, but determined to carry out his plan, wrote the following letter against the Yahuḏim:
3.12: “Meleḵ Ptolemaeus Philopator, to the commanders and soldiers in Mitsrayim and everywhere else: Greetings and good fortune!
3.13: I am well, and so are my affairs.
3.14: Since our campaign in Asia—which you know about—and which, with the help of the mighty ones and our own strength, has ended successfully as we hoped,
3.15: we decided, not by force of arms but with kindness and humanity, to care for the people of Koĕlĕ Suria and Phoinikĕ, and to be generous benefactors to them.
3.16: So, after giving large sums of money to the temples in various cities, we even went as far as Yerushalayim and went up to honor the Miqdash of these unfortunate people who never stop in their foolishness.
3.17: Outwardly, they welcomed us, but their actions showed otherwise. When we wanted to enter their Miqdash and honor it with the finest gifts,
3.18: they were so carried away by their old arrogance that they refused us entry. Yet, out of our patience with everyone, we did not use our power against them.
3.19: By doing this, they showed their hostility toward us. They alone among the nations lift their heads against melaḵim and benefactors, refusing to accept anything reasonable.
3.20: So, trying to excuse the madness of these people, and treating everyone in Mitsrayim with courtesy on our victorious return, we acted as was fitting.
3.21: Therefore, holding no grudge against their relatives, but remembering our connection with them and the many matters we have sincerely entrusted to them over a long time, we wanted to completely change their status by giving them citizenship in Alexandria and allowing them to take part in our everlasting ceremonies.
3.22: But they have responded very differently. With their natural malice, they have rejected our generous offer and always lean toward evil,
3.23: refusing these priceless rights. Not only that, but by what they say and don’t say, they despise the few among them who are friendly toward us, always thinking that their disgraceful way of life will force us to abandon our reforms.
3.24: Now that we have clear evidence that these Yahuḏim bear us every kind of ill will, we must be prepared for the possibility of a sudden uprising among us, when these wicked people might become traitors and brutal enemies.
3.25: Therefore, as soon as you receive this letter, we order that all Yahuḏim living among you, with their wives and children, be sent to us—abused and in iron chains—to suffer a cruel and shameful death, as is fitting for enemies.
3.26: By punishing them all together, we believe we have found the only way to secure our future affairs on a firm and satisfactory foundation.
3.27: Anyone who protects a Yahuḏi—whether old man, child, or nursing baby—will be tortured to death along with his entire household.
3.28: Anyone who informs on the Yahuḏim will receive, in addition to the property of the accused, two thousand drachmas from the royal treasury, will be made free, and will be crowned.
3.29: Any place that shelters a Yahuḏi will be made off-limits and destroyed by fire, and will be left useless to any living creature forever.”
3.30: The meleḵ’s letter was written in this way.

4.1: Wherever this decree was received, people broke out in loud celebrations and shouting, as if their long-held, hardened hatred was finally being unleashed openly.
4.2: The Yahuḏim suffered intense grief and wept bitterly, their hearts burning with sorrow as they mourned the sudden destruction that had been decreed against them, with everything around them filled with lament.
4.3: What home, city, inhabited place, or street was there that was not filled with their cries and mourning?
4.4: They were expelled everywhere by the generals in each city, with such harsh and merciless treatment that even some of their enemies were moved by the severity of their suffering. These, touched by basic human compassion and reflecting on the uncertainty of life, wept at the miserable expulsion of the Yahuḏim.
4.5: A multitude of elderly, gray-haired men were forced along with unsteady, shuffling steps, driven on by a violent and shameless force to move quickly.
4.6: Young women who had only recently entered the bridal chamber to enjoy marriage exchanged joy for misery; with dust scattered on their myrrh-anointed heads, they were hurried along unveiled, and in the midst of foreign insults, they all cried out in sorrow instead of singing the marriage song.
4.7: Bound and exposed to public view, they were violently rushed onto the ships.
4.8: Their husbands, in the prime of their youth, wore ropes around their necks instead of crowns. Instead of feasting and youthful celebration, they spent the rest of their wedding days in mourning, seeing only the grave ahead.
4.9: They were dragged along in unbreakable chains like wild animals. Some had their necks forced into the benches of the rowers, while others had their feet locked in heavy shackles.
4.10: The planks of the deck above blocked out the light and shut out the day on all sides, so that they were treated like traitors for the entire journey.
4.11: They were carried this way on the ship and eventually arrived at Schedia. The meleḵ had ordered them to be thrown into the large hippodrome built in front of the city. This place was perfectly situated to expose them to everyone coming into the city and those leaving for the countryside. They were completely cut off from his forces and were not considered worthy of any humane treatment.
4.12: After this, the meleḵ heard that their relatives in the city often went out and mourned the terrible suffering of these victims,
4.13: and he became furious, commanding that they be subjected to the same harsh treatment, without any mercy.
4.14: The entire nation was now to be registered. Every person was to be listed by name, not for forced labor as previously mentioned, but so he could subject them to the tortures described earlier, and finally, within a single day, destroy them through his cruelty.
4.15: The registration was carried out with cruelty, zeal, and persistence, from sunrise to sunset, and even after forty days it was not finished.
4.16: The meleḵ was filled with constant, great joy, and held banquets before the idols in the temple. His misguided heart, far from the truth, and his unclean mouth gave esteem to idols that are deaf and unable to speak or help, and he spoke unworthy words against the Most High Elohim.
4.17: At the end of this period, the officials reported to the meleḵ that the number of Yahuḏim was too great to register,
4.18: since many still remained in the land—some in inhabited houses, others scattered in different places—so that even all the commanders in Mitsrayim could not complete the task.
4.19: The meleḵ threatened them and accused them of taking bribes to help the Yahuḏim escape, but he was clearly convinced that what they said was true.
4.20: They explained and proved that they had run out of paper and pens to continue the registration.
4.21: This was actually the powerful intervention of the unconquerable Providence, which helped the Yahuḏim from the shamayim.

5.1: Then he called Hermon, who was in charge of the elephants. Filled with rage and completely set on his furious plan,
5.2: he ordered him to give the elephants a large amount of unmixed wine mixed with handfuls of incense early the next day. These five hundred elephants, once made wild by the heavy drinks of frankincense, were to be led out to put the Yahuḏim to death.
5.3: After giving these orders, the meleḵ went to his banquet and gathered all his friends and the soldiers who hated the Yahuḏim the most.
5.4: Hermon, the master of the elephants, carried out his orders exactly.
5.5: The servants assigned for this task went out in the evening, tied up the hands of the miserable victims, and took other measures to keep them secure through the night, thinking that the entire people would be destroyed together.
5.6: The nations believed the Yahuḏim had no protection at all, since they were bound in chains.
5.7: They called on 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 the Almighty, and with tears constantly begged their merciful Elohim and Father, Ruler of all, Master of every power,
5.8: to overturn the evil plan that had been made against them, and to rescue them by a miraculous sign from the death that awaited them.
5.9: Their heartfelt prayers rose up to the shamayim.
5.10: Then Hermon, who had filled his merciless elephants with large amounts of mixed wine and frankincense, came early to the palace to report on the preparations.
5.11: But He who sends sleep to His good creatures from the beginning, by night or by day, giving rest to whomever He chooses, now gave a portion of it to the meleḵ.
5.12: By this sweet and deep influence from 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, the meleḵ was held fast, and so his unjust plan was completely stopped, and his firm resolve was greatly changed.
5.13: But the Yahuḏim, having escaped the appointed hour, praised their qodesh Elohim, and again prayed to Him who is quick to forgive, asking Him to show the power of His mighty hand to the arrogant nations.
5.14: It was almost the middle of the tenth hour when the person who sent out invitations, seeing that the invited guests had arrived, came and shook the meleḵ.
5.15: He got the meleḵ’s attention with difficulty, and, hinting that the mealtime was passing, discussed the matter with him.
5.16: The meleḵ listened, then turned back to his drinking, and ordered the guests to sit down before him.
5.17: After this, he told them to enjoy themselves and to celebrate, even though it was already late in the banquet.
5.18: As the conversation continued, the meleḵ sent for Hermon and, with harsh threats, demanded to know why the Yahuḏim had survived that day.
5.19: Hermon explained that he had carried out the meleḵ’s orders the night before, and his friends confirmed this.
5.20: Then the meleḵ, with cruelty worse than Phalaris, said, “They can thank my sleep for surviving today. Don’t waste any time—get the elephants ready again for tomorrow, just as before, to destroy these cursed Yahuḏim.”
5.21: When the meleḵ said this, those present were pleased and agreed. Then each person went home.
5.22: They didn’t spend the night sleeping, but instead plotted cruel mockeries for those they considered miserable.
5.23: Just as the rooster crowed in the morning, Hermon harnessed the beasts and was urging them on in the great colonnade.
5.24: Crowds from the city gathered to witness the horrible spectacle, waiting impatiently for dawn.
5.25: The Yahuḏim, breathless with suspense, stretched out their hands and prayed to the Most High Elohim in sorrowful voices, asking Him once more to help them quickly.
5.26: The sun’s rays had not yet appeared, and the meleḵ was waiting for his friends when Hermon came to him, calling him out and saying that his wishes could now be fulfilled.
5.27: The meleḵ, receiving him, was surprised by this unusual invitation. Overcome by a spirit of forgetfulness about everything, he asked about the reason for all this urgent preparation.
5.28: But this was the work of that Almighty Elohim, who had made him forget all his plans.
5.29: Hermon and all his friends pointed out the readiness of the animals. “They are ready, O meleḵ, just as you strictly ordered.”
5.30: The meleḵ became extremely angry at these words, because by the Providence of Elohim, his mind had become completely confused. He glared at Hermon and threatened him, saying:
5.31: “If your parents or your children were here, they would have been a great meal for these wild animals, not these innocent Yahuḏim, who have faithfully served me and my ancestors.
5.32: If it weren’t for our close friendship and your official duties, your life would have been taken instead of theirs.”
5.33: Hermon, threatened so unexpectedly and alarmingly, was troubled and his face fell.
5.34: The friends also quietly left one by one, and sent the gathered crowds back to their daily work.
5.35: When the Yahuḏim heard about these events, they praised the esteemed Elohim and Meleḵ of melaḵim, because they had received this help from Him as well.
5.36: Then the meleḵ arranged another banquet in the same way and announced an invitation to celebrate.
5.37: He summoned Hermon and said with threats, “How many times, you wretch, must I repeat my orders to you about these people?
5.38: Once again, prepare the elephants for the destruction of the Yahuḏim tomorrow!”
5.39: His relatives, who were reclining with him, were amazed at his instability and said:
5.40: “O meleḵ, how long will you test us, as if we are men without sense? This is the third time you have ordered their destruction. When it is about to happen, you change your mind and cancel your instructions.
5.41: Because of this, the city is in constant turmoil and full of factions, always on the verge of chaos.”
5.42: The meleḵ, just like another Phalaris, careless and thoughtless, ignored the changes in his own mind that led to the deliverance of the Yahuḏim. He swore a useless oath and decided at once to send them to the grave, crushed by the knees and feet of the elephants.
5.43: He also planned to invade Yahuḏah, burn its towns with fire and sword, destroy that Miqdash which the nations were forbidden to enter, and stop sacrifices from ever being offered there again.
5.44: His friends and relatives joyfully broke up the meeting, and, trusting in his decision, stationed their forces at the most strategic places in the city.
5.45: The master of the elephants drove the animals into a nearly crazed state, drenched them with incense and wine, and decorated them with terrifying ornaments.
5.46: Early in the morning, when the city was packed with crowds at the hippodrome, he went into the palace and called the meleḵ to the task at hand.
5.47: The meleḵ’s heart was filled with wicked rage; he rushed out with the crowd and the elephants. With a hard heart and pitiless eyes, he was eager to see the cruel and miserable fate of the Yahuḏim mentioned before.
5.48: The elephants went out through the gate, followed by the armed forces. When the Yahuḏim saw the dust raised by the crowd and heard the loud cries,
5.49: they thought they had reached the final moment of their lives, the end they had feared. They broke down in weeping and mourning. They kissed each other. Those closest clung to one another—fathers embracing sons, mothers their daughters. Other women held their babies to their breasts, giving what seemed to be their last milk.
5.50: Yet, when they remembered the help they had received before from the shamayim, they all bowed down together, even taking the nursing children from their mothers’ breasts, and
5.51: cried out with a very loud voice, asking the Master of all power to reveal Himself and have mercy on those now lying at the gates of death.

6.1: Then Eli’ezer, a distinguished kohĕn of the land, who had reached old age and whose life was marked by uprightness, told the elders around him to stop crying out to the qodesh Elohim, and prayed this prayer:
6.2: "O Meleḵ, mighty in power, Most High, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄 the Almighty, who governs all creation with compassion,
6.3: look upon the seed of Aḇraham, the children of the qodesh Ya’aqoḇ, Your qodesh inheritance, O Father, now being unjustly destroyed as foreigners in a strange land.
6.4: You destroyed Pharaoh with his army of chariots when that ruler of this same Mitsrayim was lifted up with lawless pride and arrogant speech. By shining the light of Your mercy on the people of Yisra’ĕl, You overwhelmed him and his proud army.
6.5: When Sanḥĕriḇ, the fierce meleḵ of Ashshur, boasting in his countless army, had conquered the whole land with his spear and was lifting himself up against Your qodesh city with unbearable arrogance, You, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, destroyed him and showed Your power to many nations.
6.6: When the three friends in the land of Baḇel willingly risked their lives in the fire rather than serve worthless idols, You sent a moist coolness into the blazing furnace, and brought the fire upon all their enemies.
6.7: It was You who, when Dani’ĕl was thrown, through slander and jealousy, as prey to the lions below, brought him back unharmed into the light.
6.8: When Yonah was wasting away in the belly of the sea creature, You looked upon him, O Father, and restored him to his own people.
6.9: Now, You who hate arrogance, You who overflow with mercy, You who protect all things, appear quickly to the people of Yisra’ĕl, who are insulted by detestable, lawless nations.
6.10: If our life during our exile has been stained with sin, deliver us from the hand of the enemy, and if You will, destroy us, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, by whatever death You choose.
6.11: Do not let the proud baraḵ their vain idols over the destruction of Your beloved, saying, 'Their Elohim did not save them.'
6.12: You who are All-powerful and Almighty, O Eternal One, look! Have mercy on us who are being led away from life, like traitors, by the senseless arrogance of lawless men.
6.13: Let the nations tremble before Your invincible power today, O esteemed One, You who have all power to save the descendants of Ya’aqoḇ.
6.14: The whole assembly of children and their parents cry out to You with tears.
6.15: Let it be shown to all the nations that You are with us, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄, and have not turned Your face from us. As You said You would not forget them even in the land of their enemies, so fulfill this promise, 𐤉𐤄𐤅𐤄."
6.16: Now, as soon as Eli’ezer finished his prayer, the meleḵ came to the hippodrome with the wild animals and his noisy display of power.
6.17: When the Yahuḏim saw this, they cried out loudly to shamayim so that the nearby valleys echoed, causing an unstoppable lament throughout the army.
6.18: Then the all-esteemed, all-powerful, and true Elohim revealed His qodesh presence and opened the gates of shamayim, from which two messengers, awesome in appearance, came down and were visible to everyone except the Yahuḏim.
6.19: They stood opposite, and filled the enemy army with confusion and fear, binding them with unbreakable chains.
6.20: A cold shudder came over the meleḵ, and forgetfulness paralyzed the intensity of his spirit.
6.21: The messengers turned the animals back against the armed forces that followed them, and the animals trampled and destroyed them.
6.22: The meleḵ's anger turned into compassion, and he wept over the things he had planned.
6.23: For when he heard the cry and saw them all on the brink of destruction, he angrily threatened his friends with tears, saying,
6.24: "You have ruled badly and have been more cruel than tyrants. By secretly plotting against the reign, you have tried to deprive me, your benefactor, of both my rule and my life.
6.25: Who has gathered here, without reason removing from their homes those who, in loyalty to us, had guarded the fortresses of the land?
6.26: Who has sentenced to undeserved punishment those who, from the beginning, have shown goodwill toward us and have often risked their lives in the most dangerous situations?
6.27: Release, release the unjust bonds! Send them home in peace, asking forgiveness for what has been done.
6.28: Release the sons of the almighty living Elohim of shamayim, who from our ancestors' times until now has given us esteemed and unbroken prosperity."
6.29: He said these things, and they were released at that very moment. Having escaped death, they baraḵ Elohim, their qodesh Savior.
6.30: The meleḵ then went back to the city, called his treasurer, and ordered him to provide seven days' worth of wine and other supplies for feasting for the Yahuḏim. He decided they should celebrate a joyful festival of deliverance in the very place where they had expected to be destroyed.
6.31: Then those who had been despised and close to death—indeed, already facing it—drank the cup of deliverance instead of a bitter and sorrowful death. Filled with joy, they turned the place meant for their fall and burial into booths for feasting.
6.32: Stopping their sorrowful cries, they began to sing about their homeland, praising Elohim, their wonder-working Savior. All groaning and wailing ceased. They formed dances as a sign of peaceful joy.
6.33: So the meleḵ also gathered many guests for the occasion and gave continual thanks with great splendor for the unexpected deliverance he had received.
6.34: Those who had marked them for death and as prey, and had registered them with joy, now cried out in anguish, were covered with shame, and had the fire of their rage put out in disgrace.
6.35: But the Yahuḏim, as we have said, began to dance, and then gave themselves to feasting, joyful thanksgiving, and psalms.
6.36: They made a public decree to remember these events for generations to come, as long as they lived as sojourners. They established these days as days of rejoicing—not for drinking or excess, but because Elohim had saved them.
6.37: They asked the meleḵ to send them back to their homes.
6.38: They had been registered from the twenty-fifth of Paḵon to the fourth of Epiphi, a period of forty days. The measures for their destruction lasted from the fifth of Epiphi to the seventh, that is, three days.
6.39: The Ruler over all showed His mercy with great esteem during this time, and delivered them all together unharmed.
6.40: They enjoyed the meleḵ's provisions until the fourteenth day, then asked to be sent away.
6.41: The meleḵ praised them and wrote the following letter, of great generosity toward them, to the commanders of every city:

7.1: Meleḵ Ptolemaeus Philopator to the commanders throughout Mitsrayim, and to all those in charge of affairs: joy and strength.
7.2: We and our children are well. Elohim has guided our affairs as we desired.
7.3: Some of our friends, out of malice, strongly urged us to punish the Yahuḏim in our reign with a terrible punishment.
7.4: They claimed that our affairs would never prosper until this was done, saying that the Yahuḏim hated all other peoples.
7.5: They brought them in heavy chains as slaves—no, as traitors—without any inquiry or investigation, trying to destroy them. They acted with a cruelty even worse than Skuthian customs.
7.6: Because of this, we threatened them severely; yet, with the mercy we usually show to all, we finally allowed the Yahuḏim to live. Seeing that the Elohim of shamayim protected the Yahuḏim and preserved them, and that He fought for them as a father fights for his sons,
7.7: and considering their loyalty and faithfulness to us and our ancestors, we have, as we should, cleared them of every accusation.
7.8: We have sent them back to their homes, instructing everyone everywhere not to harm them or unjustly insult them about the past.
7.9: Know this: if we ever plan evil against them or harm them in any way, our adversary will not be a man, but the Most High Elohim, the ruler of all power. There will be no escape from Him, as He avenges such actions. Farewell.
7.10: When they received this letter, they did not rush to leave immediately. They asked the meleḵ for permission to punish those of their own people who had willingly transgressed against the qodesh Elohim and the Torah.
7.11: They argued that those who had broken Elohim’s commands for the sake of their appetites would never be loyal to the meleḵ’s interests.
7.12: The meleḵ agreed with their reasoning and praised them. He gave them full authority, without any special order, to destroy those who had boldly broken the Torah of Elohim throughout his reign.
7.13: Their kohenim, as was fitting, acclaimed him, and all the people shouted, “Hallelu-Yah!” Then they left with joy.
7.14: They then punished and shamefully destroyed every defiled Yahuḏi they found.
7.15: That day, they killed more than three hundred men, considering the destruction of the wicked a time of joy.
7.16: Having remained faithful to their Elohim even to death and having received complete deliverance, they left the city crowned with sweet-flowered wreaths of every kind. With shouts of joy, songs of praise, and melodious hymns, they thanked the Elohim of their fathers, the eternal Savior of Yisra’ĕl.
7.17: When they arrived at Ptolemais, known in that region as 'Rose-bearing,' where the fleet waited for them for seven days as everyone wished,
7.18: they celebrated a banquet of deliverance, for the meleḵ generously provided everything they needed to return home.
7.19: They were brought back in peace, giving thanks as was fitting, and decided to observe these days as days of joy during their stay.
7.20: They recorded these days as qodesh on a pillar, after dedicating the place of their celebration as one of prayer. They departed unharmed, free, full of joy, protected by the meleḵ’s command—by land, sea, and river—each to his own home.
7.21: They were more respected than before among their enemies, and were honored and feared. No one took their possessions in any way.
7.22: Everyone received back what belonged to him, according to the records, and those who had taken their goods returned them in great fear. For the Most High Elohim performed perfect wonders for their deliverance.
7.23: Baruḵ be the Redeemer of Yisra’ĕl forever! Amĕn.
